title: Carbon dioxide is rising, and rising faster
slideTitles: Carbon dioxide is rising, and rising faster
Carbon dioxide in the air keeps climbing.
The curve breathes once a year.
The climb is steeper now than in the 1960s.
Half the rise came in the last 23 years.

states.lead: Carbon dioxide above Mauna Loa, every month.
states.body: Monthly means in parts per million, from March 1958. Scripps data to April 1974, NOAA after.
That is March 1958, the first month of C. David Keeling's record.
The highest monthly mean in the record so far.

states.lead: Up close, the line is a sawtooth.
Highs in late spring, lows in early fall.
states.body: Every year peaked in May or June and bottomed out in September or October.

states.lead: Growing plants pull carbon dioxide down.
states.body: Respiration and decay release it again. Each yearly swing ran 4.9 to 6.1 ppm.

states.lead: Each bar is a decade's average yearly rise.
states.body: NOAA annual growth at Mauna Loa, averaged across each decade, in ppm per year.

states.lead: In the 2010s, it rose 2.8 times as fast.
states.body: Measured against the 1960s, the first full decade of the record.

states.lead: This decade is running faster still.
states.body: 6 years in, the average rise is 2.56 ppm a year.
Yearly averages, from 315.98 ppm in 1959 to 427.35 in 2025.
The first half of the rise took 43 years. The second half took 23.

states.lead: Every year beat the one before.
states.body: No annual average since 1959 has fallen below the previous year's.
